result:
I woke up to the sound of the radiator clicking on, a little metallic cough that means the building is warming itself before anyone else is awake. The light through the blinds is thin and yellow, like it’s been filtered through old paper. I lie there for a minute and listen to my own breathing and to the city outside the window which never really sleeps, it just changes volume.

Coffee is the first real decision of the day. I pour water into the kettle and watch the little bubbles climb the sides of the glass. It’s stupidly soothing. While it boils I open the curtains and the whole street is suddenly there, wet from last night, a dog walker with a reflective vest, a delivery truck idling. The world looks freshly printed.

I think about how much of my life is made of these tiny repetitions. Toothbrush, kettle, key in the lock. And yet inside those repetitions there is a constant drift. The plant on the windowsill is a little taller than it was last week. The chipped mug I always use has a new chip near the rim. I’m different, obviously, but in such small increments you don’t notice until someone points it out.

Work is a screen and a chair and a list that never ends. I make a to-do list and then immediately feel tired by looking at it. The first email is always from someone polite and urgent. I answer it with a tone I have practiced, calm and helpful, even though I am thinking about the kettle at home and whether I left the window open.

There is a bird that lives in the gutter outside my apartment. It’s a pigeon, I think, or maybe a starling. It makes this sound like a squeaky hinge. I have named it in my head, but I won’t tell anyone the name because naming makes it too real and then if it disappears it will be a small grief. It’s probably just a bird. It’s just a bird that I have been watching for three months.

At lunch I walk without a destination. The air smells like rain and bus exhaust and someone frying onions two blocks over. I buy a sandwich I won’t remember later and eat it on a bench while people pass. A kid on a scooter wobbles, a woman reads a paperback with a cracked spine, a man in a suit talks loudly into his phone about numbers. I feel both inside it and outside it, like I’m watching a film of my own day.

I keep thinking about time. How it feels longer in the morning and then it compresses in the afternoon into a blur. I have a friend who says we should waste time more intentionally. I think about that while I’m standing in line at the pharmacy. The line moves slowly. I could be doing something productive. I am not. I am just standing. Maybe that is the waste. Maybe that is the point.

The evening comes in through the kitchen window. The light gets amber and then blue. I make pasta because it’s easy and forgiving. I burn the garlic a little and add too much salt and then I fix it with lemon. It tastes fine. It tastes like home, which is mostly a collection of small corrections.

I read a few pages before bed. Fiction, because nonfiction feels too much like work. There is a character in this book who is trying to remember something they lost and they keep circling around it without ever naming it. I recognize that feeling. It’s not about memory, really. It’s about the shape the absence leaves.

The radiator clicks off. The building is done for the night. I turn the lamp down low and the room becomes a softer version of itself. I think about tomorrow, which will be much like today, and I don’t mind that. There is comfort in the repetition and also a quiet surprise in it, the way the light changes, the way the bird is still in the gutter, the way I am still here to notice.

If I could say one thing to myself from this moment, it would be to keep paying attention to small things. The kettle. The chip in the mug. The way the street looks after rain. They are not important in any grand sense, but they are the texture of being alive, and I want to remember the texture.

I’m tired now. The words are starting to loop. I should stop writing and let the day settle. The ceiling has a small crack that looks like a river. I’ll watch it for a minute before sleep finds me.
